Urban Core Industry

Data–Manufacturing–Power Generation–Workforce Housing Campus

Two campuses in Cleveland's urban core that put data halls, advanced manufacturing, on-site power generation and workforce housing on one site — built on land that is already largely held in public land banks. Power goes in first and is built once. Cooling lives inside and on top of vertical data towers, with no ground-level cooling yard. Every displaced household is offered a new house on a nearby vacant lot, built before demolition begins, and the territory stays owned by Cleveland taxpayers.

Heat recovery

HRSG — Heat Recovery Steam Generator

A gas turbine on its own sends more than a third of its fuel energy out the stack as exhaust above 1,000 °F. The HRSG is the large heat exchanger that sits in that exhaust path and puts the heat back to work. Its tube banks boil water into high-pressure steam that drives a steam turbine — the second half of a combined cycle, adding power without burning any more fuel. At the cool end of the HRSG, an economizer and hot-water heat exchanger pull out the heat that is left and deliver hot water to a campus loop.

017HA.03 turbine exhaust
02HRSG tube banks make steam
03Steam turbine adds power
04Economizer heats water
05Hot water loop to the campus
More power

Steam from the HRSG lifts a 430 MW simple-cycle turbine to roughly 640 MW in combined cycle, at about 64% efficiency.

Hot water

Recovered heat supplies a district hot-water loop for space heating and domestic hot water in workforce housing, retail and offices, and process heat for manufacturing — heat a boiler would otherwise have to burn fuel to make.

Chilled water

In summer the same hot water drives absorption chillers, turning waste heat into cooling for the campus buildings.

Coming soon

GE Vernova BWRX-300 SMR Nuclear Power Plant

The BWRX-300 is a 300-megawatt small modular reactor from GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy — the tenth generation of GE's boiling water reactor, built as a simplified, smaller version of the NRC-certified ESBWR. Water circulates through the core by natural circulation, with no recirculation pumps, and passive isolation condensers can remove decay heat for seven days without operator action or outside power. It is carbon-free, firm baseload that can also supply heat for district heating and hydrogen production — the long-term successor to gas as the anchor of our campuses.

Output300 MWe · 870 MWt per unit

Community protection

Quiet by Design. Watched Around the Clock.

Every campus and system design is equipped with triple-layer noise mitigation and a 24-hour monitoring system, along with environmental impact mitigation — standards that should be specified and enforced by every municipality.
Triple-layer noise mitigation
LAYER 01 · SOURCE

Contain It at the Equipment

Turbines sit inside double-wall acoustic super-enclosures. HRSG casings are clad and sealed, stacks are fully lined with vertical silencers, ducts carry splitter silencers, and cooling fans are oversized to run at low RPM behind discharge silencers.

LAYER 02 · PATH

Block It Across the Site

The power block sits in the middle of the campus inside a continuous earth berm and wall ring. Data halls, manufacturing bays and office buildings are placed to act as shields, so no line of sight runs from a noise source to a home.

LAYER 03 · PERIMETER

Buffer It at the Neighborhood Edge

A landscaped setback with a vegetation buffer and a solid concrete wall runs along every residential edge. Designs target 50–55 dBC at the perimeter at night — measuring the low-frequency hum that standard dBA limits miss.

24-hour monitoring
  • Perimeter sound stationsContinuous dBA and dBC readings at every residential edge, day and night
  • Night limits in the controlsFan speeds are capped from 10 pm to 6 am inside the control system, not left to a written procedure
  • Emissions and airContinuous emissions monitoring on every turbine stack
  • Public dataLive readings published for residents, with alerts when a limit is approached
  • Baseline firstA full week of measured day-and-night sound before anything is built, so every promise is checked against the real neighborhood
Environmental impact mitigation
  • WaterDry, air-cooled heat rejection and closed-loop cooling — no evaporative cooling towers and no visible plume
  • AirSCR emissions control in every HRSG, with natural gas primary and a hydrogen blend reducing carbon at peak
  • Waste heatRecovered as hot water for housing, retail and manufacturing instead of sent up the stack
  • StormwaterOn-site detention sized to the campus, and vegetation buffers that cool the edge and filter runoff
  • DischargePretreatment of any process water to sewer-district standards before it leaves the site
What every municipality should specify and enforce
01Night and day limits in both dBA and dBC, measured at the property line
02A measured baseline before any permit is issued
03Continuous monitoring with data published to the public
04Independent verification and enforceable penalties, up to curtailment
